Kill criteria and decision rules

Deciding in advance what result ends the idea — and what it costs when the rule is written in the wrong currency.

1. Two signatures, three weeks apart

On Wednesday 14 January 2026, Tanmay Wadekar put a sheet of paper in front of Zenara Money's chief financial officer, Tarini Welankar, and asked her to sign it. Zenara was a Bengaluru consumer credit application with 94,00,000 registered users, built on the bureau rails TransUnion CIBIL and Experian provide to every Indian lender. The sheet set out a decision rule for Zuraksha, a ₹399-a-year subscription bundling bureau-score monitoring with assisted dispute resolution, costed at ₹1.90 crore. Of the 7,200 eligible users shown a payment-capable offer page, 211 or more paid subscribers would approve the build and 165 or fewer would cancel it; anything between bought one extension, not a reprieve. Neither signatory would amend the sheet afterwards.

Welankar signed. What interested her was not the number 211 but that it had a derivation she could read: two previous launches had been approved on enthusiastic qualitative research and then defended, quarter after quarter, against results that never quite arrived. "I have never minded being wrong," she said. "I have minded not being able to say on what date we learned it."

Nine months later, on Monday 12 October 2026, Tanaz Wadhera faced the same question with almost none of the same equipment. Wadhera was director of product at Zevaar Industrial Systems, a Pune firm selling retrofit instrumentation and analytics for compressed-air systems in the textile and auto-component clusters of Tiruppur and Chakan. Her product, Zurekha, had finished a nine-month paid pilot in six plants costing ₹1.08 crore — ₹57.00 lakh of kits at cost, ₹34.00 lakh of field engineering, ₹8.40 lakh of travel and instrumentation, ₹8.60 lakh of data work — and the decision was whether to commit ₹4.20 crore to industrialisation — tooling, Bureau of Indian Standards certification and a field team — for an August 2027 launch. Her kill criterion, signed on 4 February 2026 and countersigned by Theodora Wolseley, Zevaar's commercial lead in London, read: proceed if four or more of the six plants order at eighty-five per cent of list within sixty days of pilot close; stop if one or fewer do; if two or three do, extend with three further pilots. By 12 October three plants had ordered, one had refused, and two were waiting on capital budgets that reset in April.

Wadekar's rule decided. Wadhera's landed, with a probability she had never computed, exactly where it was least useful. The difference is not courage: one rule was written in a currency the test could settle in, the other was not. What follows turns on that, and on the three places kill criteria fail — the denominator, the resolution, and the authority.

2. The idea, and the four positions people hold about it

A kill criterion is a result, specified before data collection, whose occurrence ends work on an idea. A decision rule is the larger object: a mapping from every outcome to an action — stop, continue, extend, build — plus the base the outcome is measured over, the date it is read, who may overturn it, and what overturning costs them. The kill criterion is one cell; most of the difficulty lives in the others.

The problem it solves is not ignorance but motivated interpretation. Barry Staw's experiments in the mid-1970s established escalation of commitment: subjects allocated more to a course of action precisely because they had chosen it and it was failing. Isabelle Royer's 2003 field studies added the social layer: projects were sustained by a collective belief that made doubt socially expensive. Clinical trials answered this with pre-registered outcomes and stopping boundaries, and the sequential-analysis literature — Armitage, then Pocock, then O'Brien and Fleming — exists to price the act of looking at data more than once. Robert Cooper's Stage-Gate research distinguished firms with "gates that have teeth" from those whose gates were tollgates everything passed. And McGrath and MacMillan's 1995 discovery-driven planning supplied the direct ancestor: a reverse income statement, an assumption checklist, and milestones chosen to test the assumption whose failure would most change the plan.

Where serious practitioners disagree is over what a pre-committed threshold is for.

Both critiques are correct, and point in opposite directions.

3. Mechanics: five steps, and the two always skipped

Expert practice runs five steps in order: name the assumption the money rests on; derive the threshold from the economics; translate it into what the test can measure; check the test can resolve it; fix the authority. The first and last are the ones teams skip; the fourth separates a rule from a wish. For Zuraksha the assumption was not "users want to monitor their credit score" but enough eligible users will pay ₹399 that the build returns its cost within twenty-four months. Then the denominator, which Wable got wrong on his first pass. He divided 47,697 by Zenara's 94,00,000 registered users, giving a required take-up of 0.51 per cent — so low almost any result would clear it. But registered users were not eligible: Zuraksha needed a live bureau-pull consent and a credit facility to monitor. Because the page charged money, the measured act was the business act and no transfer coefficient was needed — the main advantage of a priced smoke test over a fake door. Below roughly five to one the test's own cost belongs inside the rule.

Step four requires a stated convention, because "2.9 per cent" is not a decision input until you say what its uncertainty entitles you to do.

Build only if the one-sided 95 per cent lower confidence bound on paid take-up (normal approximation, z = 1.645, on the observed proportion) clears break-even of 2.592 per cent. Kill if the one-sided 95 per cent upper bound falls below it — if even the optimistic reading misses. Otherwise extend once to 14,400 and reapply.

Second-order effects

First, the extension is not free. At n = 14,400 the recomputed cuts are k ≤ 343 for kill (upper bound 2.5910 per cent) and k ≥ 406 for build (lower bound 2.5925 per cent), and the gap between the two cuts narrows from 0.639 to 0.437 percentage points. But two looks at a nominal one-sided five per cent are not a five per cent standard. Computed exactly — binomial on the first 7,200, then on the cumulative 14,400 after a further independent 7,200 — a product at break-even produces a build verdict 7.0 per cent of the time against 4.0 per cent for a single look. This is what Pocock's and O'Brien and Fleming's boundaries correct.

Second, the rule changes the test's design before it changes any decision. Once a threshold exists the instrument becomes load-bearing, and teams face a quiet incentive to shift the metric toward something easier to clear — from "paid" to "tapped Subscribe", from eligible base to rendered base. The diagnostic is mechanical: is the rule's metric the one named in the assumption, over the same base? Third, the rule is a promise to the team: a kill under a pre-signed criterion reads as a rule honoured, a kill without one as politics — and the second kind costs an organisation its best people.

The practice is actively misleading in three situations. Where the dominant risk is feasibility or regulatory rather than demand, a demand threshold is a category error — Zevaar's may be whether a retrofit passes a plant's electrical safety audit, a binary with no rate. Where the item will be built regardless, a kill criterion teaches the organisation that rules are theatre. And under cold-start effects, early rates measure the cold start, not the product.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature companies actually do

Features inside a bundle. A standalone threshold is wrong where value is partly cross-elastic. Zenara's holdout suggested Zuraksha lifted twelve-month retention of the lending product: 1,332 of 1,860 treated users retained against 1,294 of 1,840 controls, a difference of 1.2868 percentage points. Across the eligible base that is 23,677 of 18,40,000 users, worth ₹151.53 lakh at ₹640 of twelve-month contribution each — enough to cut the effective build cost to ₹38.47 lakh and break-even take-up from 2.59 to 0.52 per cent. But the standard error of that difference is √(0.7161 × 0.2839 ÷ 1,860 + 0.7033 × 0.2967 ÷ 1,840) = 1.492 percentage points, so the two-sided 95 per cent interval (z = 1.96) runs from −1.64 to +4.21 percentage points. The lift is indistinguishable from zero; importing it would smuggle noise into the threshold dressed as strategy.

Two-sided markets. A criterion on one side is incomplete and the base problem is acute. The binding quantity is the match rate, and the characteristic defect is that requests arriving where no eligible supply existed within the radius were never logged as unmet demand, so the denominator excludes the failures that matter most. Define the base from the launch footprint, not the log.

Regulated products. A compliance-driven item cannot be killed, so it carries a scope rule, not a kill rule; and with a bank partner under the Reserve Bank's digital-lending framework the read-out date is the partner's credit committee's, not yours.

Hardware plus software, and the seam that broke Wadhera's rule. Zevaar's tooling order was ₹96.00 lakh with an ₹18.00 lakh non-refundable deposit and a fourteen-week lead time, and had to be placed by 15 March 2027 for an August 2027 launch. The first-pass order deadline of 29 November 2026 sits before that; the grey branch does not. Three further pilots at full list would start in January 2027, close at the end of July and produce orders in late September — 198 days, six and a half months, after the tooling door closes.

AI-native products. The subject of the test moves while you test it: a model upgrade mid-window changes the thing measured, and quality is multidimensional with no single rate to threshold. Expert practice freezes the model version and the evaluation set inside the rule, and names which upgrades reopen the question.

What mature companies actually do. They say they have kill criteria. Most have a quarterly reallocation ritual in which nothing is killed and some things are not re-funded, the kill executed as a staffing decision weeks later. At portfolio scale a re-funding rule is often the more honest instrument; the failure is pretending the two are the same, so nobody writes the criterion and nobody takes the gate seriously.

6. Four nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

1. The number to argue about is the operating characteristic, not the threshold.
Competent practitioners negotiate the threshold; experts compute, before running anything, the probability of each action under each truth that would change the decision. Tell-tale sign: the first question about a new rule is "what happens if the truth is just above break-even?", not "is 2.6 the right number?" The obvious reading — that a precise threshold buys decisiveness — is wrong: decisiveness comes from resolution, which the threshold does not touch.
2. A kill criterion is a claim about a denominator before it is a claim about a rate.
Every recorded base error in this topic was a denominator including units never eligible, or measured over a different window than the numerator. Tell-tale sign: the expert spends forty minutes on eligibility and five on the number. The test is physical, not statistical: how many units in the base were able to perform the measured act, on a device and in a state that permitted it?
3. Pre-commitment draws its power from the cost of overturning, not from the writing.
A rule its authors can amend quietly is a preference. Tell-tale sign: the expert asks who signs, who must be present to overturn it, and what overturning costs them in visibility. Zenara's sheet had a clause nobody noticed: any amendment required Welankar's initials and a written reason, circulated to the original list. In nine months it has never been amended — not because the clause was enforced but because it made amendment awkward.
4. Choose the convention so the expensive error is the rare one — and check which error is expensive.
One-sided or two-sided, and which z, allocates the error. Zenara required the lower bound to clear break-even, making a false build rare and a false kill likelier — appropriate when cash is tight and the idea is replaceable. Tell-tale sign: the expert states both error costs in rupees before choosing the convention. The common mistake is assuming the false continue is always the expensive one; section 8c says otherwise by a factor of 2.75. The same logic makes "extend" a priced decision, not a safe harbour: it is the only branch that commits money without deciding anything.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

Two of the usual differences are real. In consumer products with large bases and cheap instrumentation, thresholds can be statistical and read in days — Zuraksha's rule is possible only because 7,200 renders cost ₹11.20 lakh. In enterprise and industrial products the sample is a dozen accounts at most, so the criterion must be denominated in costly commitments, and its error rates will be embarrassing however written. In hardware the binding constraint is lead time rather than evidence: the rule must fire before tooling, certification or inventory commits, so the data must be engineered to arrive earlier, usually by paying for a smaller, worse, earlier read. In marketplaces the criterion belongs on the match; in AI products it must name a frozen model and evaluation set.

What does not differ, though exemption is often claimed: the obligation to derive the threshold from economics, the eligibility-checked denominator, and the independent signatory. A team claiming exemption for being enterprise, or early, or regulated is usually exempting itself from the derivation rather than the statistics. Stage changes the instrument, not the discipline: a seed-stage rule is one sentence on a whiteboard with a date and a signatory.

8. Three worked examples

8a. Zuraksha: a rule that decided, by one subscriber

The offer page ran from 2 to 16 February 2026 to a random sample of the eligible base, with 7,200 confirmed renders. On 17 February the count was 212 of 7,200 users, a paid take-up of 2.94 per cent, whose lower bound of 2.6167 per cent cleared break-even by 0.024 percentage points. Wable then recomputed under a different convention: a one-sided 95 per cent Wilson score bound, which handles small proportions better than the normal approximation, gives 2.6340 per cent — slightly higher, so the verdict holds. But Wilson moves every cut, not one: at 7,200 to k ≤ 164 and k ≥ 209, a grey zone of 165 to 208; at 14,400 to k ≤ 341 and k ≥ 405. Direction matters too. At break-even the exact binomial puts 4.04 per cent of outcomes at or above the Wald build cut but 5.63 per cent at or below the kill cut, so the published rule is conservative about building and anti-conservative about killing — the wrong way round for a company whose own false kill cost 2.75 times its false continue.

Wadekar's reading was not "validated" but "not killed": a rule cleared by one subscriber produced a verdict, not a confident estimate. That shaped the launch — a staged release with a second, post-launch criterion: if ninety-day paid retention on the first 20,000 subscribers falls below 68 per cent, Zuraksha is sunset by 30 November 2026.

8c. Zubaan: the rule that worked as written, and cost ₹1.71 crore

In 2025 Zenara tested Zubaan, a Kannada, Telugu and Tamil voice layer over the app's loan-status and payment flows. Tanvi Wagholikar, then its product manager, wrote the criterion in advance: kill unless at least 18 per cent of users in the test cell complete a loan-status enquiry by voice within fourteen days. The cell was 11,900 users; the result was 1,357 of 11,900 users, or 11.4 per cent. She killed it in four days and was praised for it.

Two things were wrong, and only the second inverted the decision. First the base: 3,480 users in the cell were on Android builds where the microphone permission prompt silently failed, so they were never able to perform the measured act. The eligible base was 8,420, and 1,357 of 8,420 users is 16.1 per cent — still below 18, which is why it went unexamined for eleven months. Second, and fatally: the 18 per cent had no provenance; it was the adoption rate of the app's existing chat-support feature, borrowed as a benchmark. The derivation nobody ran is three lines, and its inputs — ₹38 a call, 4.0 calls a year, a fourteen-day enquiry read as sustained use — are stipulations. The build was ₹62.00 lakh; each voice enquiry avoided a support call costing ₹38; a voice-adopting user was expected to replace 4.0 calls a year, so contribution per adopter was ₹152 a year. Twelve-month payback needed 62,00,000 ÷ 152 = 40,789 adopters, and against the Indian-language segment that is 40,789 of 22,70,000 users, or 1.80 per cent. Comparing 16.1 per cent with that would repeat this section's own error: 1.80 per cent is computed over the whole segment, 16.1 per cent over the eligible base alone. Like for like, the cell's 11.4 per cent is 6.3 times break-even. The rule had killed a product clearing its own business case six times over, with perfect procedural integrity.

Almost nobody keeps one, because killed projects generate no data, and a firm that never audits its kills can only learn about its false continues.

9. Four failure modes and their early warning signs

The borrowed threshold.
Early sign: the number is round — twenty per cent, one in three — and its proposer says "roughly industry". Diagnostic: which line of the business case is it from? Cost late: Zubaan, ₹170.79 lakh.
The ineligible denominator.
Early sign: the instrumented base and the eligibility-defined base differ and nobody has reconciled them in writing. Diagnostic: how many units were physically able to act, and when did their clock start? Cost late: a verdict of 11.4 per cent on a true 16.1 per cent, unappealable because the arithmetic was consistent.
The unresolvable rule.
Early sign: the pre-computed cuts are far apart relative to the sample, or the sample is a dozen accounts. Diagnostic: under each truth that would change our action, what is the probability the rule produces it? Cost late: Zurekha — a decision made on exhaustion, and the practice discredited as "the rule didn't help".
The decision date that precedes the data date.
Early sign: a long-lead irreversible commitment — tooling, certification, an inventory buy — with a deadline inside or before the test window. Diagnostic: on what date does money become unrecoverable, and when does the read-out land? Cost late: Zevaar's ₹18.00 lakh deposit, or a one-year slip.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Should a rule bind when the prior moves for off-test reasons? The pre-commitment position, steelmanned: the instrument's entire value is that it cannot be relitigated, and every exception clause is a door escalation walks through — the clinical-trial literature exists because flexible analysis reliably manufactures favourable findings, and Royer's evidence shows the mechanism is social. The decision-theoretic position, steelmanned: a rule is adopted because it beats the average ad-hoc decision, not every informed one, and if a competitor ships the feature mid-test, refusing to update is a refusal to use information. For the first to be wrong, organisations updating mid-test would have to not systematically update in the direction they already wanted; for the second, off-test information arriving mid-test would have to be mostly noise. Neither has been shown.

Per-experiment criteria, or portfolio re-funding gates? The portfolio position: most individual experiments cannot resolve their own thresholds — Table 7 is the general case — so per-experiment criteria mostly manufacture false kills, false continues and grey zones, while a re-funding gate forces the comparison against the alternative use of the people. The per-experiment position: gates that review everything review nothing, Cooper's research distinguishes gates with teeth from tollgates, and the per-experiment criterion is the only instrument that fires before sunk cost accumulates, when the bias is weakest. Settling it needs evidence on whether firms with explicit criteria earn better portfolio returns than firms with disciplined quarterly re-funding; that comparison has not been run.

Statistical thresholds or commitment evidence at low n? The commitment-evidence position: with six plants the statistics are theatre, and one order at full list with an advance carries more information than any rate computed on six. The statistical position: an order is also a sample of one from a population you selected, and the pilots' enthusiasm is the selection bias a transfer coefficient corrects — Zevaar's 0.362 rests on 12 warm and 94 cold cases. Both are weak; the disagreement is which weakness is recoverable.

Do kill criteria improve portfolios or degrade them? For: escalation of commitment is among the best-documented biases in organisational behaviour, and pre-commitment is the only intervention that has reliably reduced it. Against: kill criteria select for ideas that clear a threshold quickly and cheaply, the wrong selection if returns are heavy-tailed — the ideas worth most are those whose early signal is weakest, so a firm that kills efficiently may have traded its tail for its mean. Settling it would require showing that ideas killed early would not have produced outsized returns; because killed projects generate no counterfactual, that is close to unfalsifiable, which is why the disagreement persists.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this writes a threshold and feels protected. Someone who has internalised it writes the rule before designing the test and lets it choose the test — which is how a priced page displaces a fake door. They argue about the denominator for an hour and the threshold for five minutes. They compute the operating characteristic before running anything, and will say what competent practitioners almost never say: this test cannot answer this question at any sample we can afford — a conclusion, not a failure. And they audit their kills, looking for the Zubaan: the thing killed correctly by a rule that was itself wrong. Only the last is rare, and it is the one that compounds.

12. What each of them decided

On 19 February 2026 Wadekar recommended the build and Welankar approved it, both on record describing the verdict as "not killed" rather than validated. The rule had been honoured, the conclusion survived a Wilson recomputation, and a marginal verdict warranted a staged launch with a second kill criterion on ninety-day paid retention — written before the launch, for the same reason as the first.

On 12 October 2026 Wadhera did neither of the things her rule allowed: she did not proceed on three orders, and she did not kill. She told Wolseley and Tobias Wernicke, Zevaar's certification lead in Stuttgart, that the rule had been written in the wrong currency and that she proposed to replace it rather than overturn it — a distinction she insisted on in writing. The replacement moved the evidence from counts to terms, on the timetable section 8b sets out. Whether replacing a rule one has signed is discipline or escalation in better clothes is the question her board asked.

  1. Wadhera's rule was correctly derived and unusable. When should that have been visible, and who was accountable for noticing it?
  2. Zuraksha cleared its build cut by one subscriber. Is a verdict from a margin of one conversion a good rule, a lucky one, or an argument for a wider grey band? Answer from Table 4, not intuition.
  3. Zenara audits its kill log annually, but killed projects generate no counterfactual. What evidence could it produce, and what would make it change a threshold rather than reassure the people who set it?

13. Going deeper

Designing discovery experiments — the rule should choose the test, not follow it. Portfolio kill criteria and stage gates — the unit of decision becomes the funding cycle, where section 10's second disagreement is fought. The four product risks — each needs a different kind of threshold. Landing-page and smoke tests — the cheapest instrument that can carry a statistical threshold. Fake doors and painted doors — where the transfer coefficient becomes unavoidable. Concierge and Wizard of Oz tests — low-n instruments needing qualitative stopping conditions. Pre-sales, LOIs and deposits — the currencies that make a low-n rule settle. Prototype testing — where borrowed benchmarks are commonest of all.
exp20v2-val.kill:
Kill criteria and decision rules

What result would make us stop, and did we decide that before running the test?

1. A Tuesday in June

On Tuesday 9 June 2026, Sreeja Vaidyanathan, head of product at Zalmar Health, a pharmacy-delivery app of the kind that competes with Tata 1mg, PharmEasy and Apollo 24/7, sat down with her chief financial officer, Satya Vemparala, to approve a build. The proposal was ZoRefill: a feature that would let a customer on long-term medication (blood-pressure tablets, diabetes drugs, thyroid replacement) tick one box and have the pharmacy refill and deliver the prescription every month without being asked. The engineering estimate was four months and ₹60 lakh. Zalmar had 3,20,000 customers who had bought chronic medication at least twice in the previous six months, and the sales team believed a large share of them would say yes.

Vemparala did not dispute the idea. His objection was narrower: the previous two launches had each been approved on the strength of an enthusiastic pilot, and each had then been defended, quarter after quarter, against numbers that never quite arrived. "I do not mind being wrong," he said. "I mind not knowing when we learned we were wrong." Vaidyanathan proposed a two-week fake-door test (a button for a feature that does not yet exist, which records the click and then thanks the customer for their interest). She also proposed something less usual: that before a single customer saw the button, the two of them would write down, and sign, the click rate below which the build would be cancelled.

The decision at stake was ₹60 lakh and four engineers for four months. The subtler risk was what would happen if the result landed in the grey zone and nobody had said in advance what grey meant. This page follows that signature, and what it did and did not protect against.

2. The idea

A kill criterion is a result, stated before a test is run, that will cause the team to stop work on an idea. A decision rule is the larger object around it: a written mapping from every plausible outcome of the test to an action, such as kill, continue, extend the test, or build. The problem both solve is that people interpret evidence after seeing it, and interpretation bends toward what they already want. A team that has spent six weeks on an idea, and has told the board about it, will find a reading of almost any data that justifies a seventh week.

The discipline has two older relatives. Clinical trials learned to register their primary outcome and stopping rules in advance, because trials analysed without such rules found benefits with suspicious regularity; journals began demanding registration in the early 2000s. Industrial stage-gate processes, popularised from the 1980s, learned to attach explicit pass-or-stop tests to each stage for a different reason: projects acquire momentum, and momentum is not evidence. Product discovery borrowed both.

The sentence Vaidyanathan could repeat in any meeting: "We are not asking whether this might work; we are agreeing today what result would convince us that it does not."

3. How it works, step by step

The mechanics are short, but several steps are usually left implicit. First, name the single assumption the whole investment rests on. For ZoRefill it was not "customers like convenience" (nearly everyone does) but "enough eligible customers will commit to a recurring order that the build pays back within twelve months." Second, convert that assumption into the quantity the test can measure and the threshold that quantity must reach: this is the step that needs arithmetic, and it is where most teams skip. Third, adjust for the gap between what the test measures and what the business needs, because a click is not a subscription. Fourth, set the decision zones. Fifth, write the rule down, get the person who controls the money to sign it, and fix the sample size. Only then run the test.

The implicit steps deserve emphasis. Step 3, the discount, is where optimism hides: a fake-door click costs the customer nothing, so it overstates real commitment. Step 5 is not a formality either. A rule that its authors can amend after the data arrive is a preference, not a rule. The protection comes from the cost of changing it: a signed page that must be visibly overturned in front of the person who signed it.

4. A worked example, line by line

Vaidyanathan and her analyst, Shruti Venkataraghavan, began with the economics. Each automatic refill earned Zalmar a contribution (revenue less medicine cost, delivery and payment fees) of ₹95. Past subscription products suggested a customer who signed up would complete 7.2 refills in the first twelve months, allowing for people who stop. Twelve-month contribution per subscriber was therefore 95 × 7.2 = ₹684. Against a build cost of ₹60,00,000, break-even needed 60,00,000 ÷ 684 = 8,772 subscribers (rounded up), which is 8,772 ÷ 3,20,000 = 2.74 per cent of the eligible base.

The test, however, would measure clicks, not subscribers. Zalmar had run two earlier fake-door tests on features later built, and in both the eventual paid take-up was a fraction of the click rate: 0.31 in one, 0.49 in the other, an average of 0.40. Dividing the needed 2.74 per cent by 0.40 gave a break-even click rate of 6.85 per cent. Satya Vemparala then asked how sure the team needed to be before cancelling. They agreed on a one-sided 90 per cent standard: kill only if even the optimistic end of the estimate falls short of break-even. With 2,400 randomly chosen eligible customers shown the card, the optimistic end of an observed 6.0 per cent is 6.0% + 1.645 × √(0.06 × 0.94 ÷ 2,400) = 6.0% + 0.80% = 6.80 per cent, just under 6.85. So the zones were fixed as follows.

ZoneClicks out of 2,400 who saw the cardClick rateAction
Kill144 or fewer6.0% or lowerCancel the ₹60 lakh build
Extend145 to 167above 6.0%, below 7.0%One extension only: show the card to 2,400 more, then apply the closing rule in the last row to the combined 4,800
Build168 or more7.0% or higherApprove the build
Closing rule after the extension (4,800 customers)301 or fewer / 302 or more6.27% or lower / above301 or fewer: cancel. 302 or more: build. There is no second extension.

The denominator is customers for whom the card was confirmed rendered, not app opens or customers selected. At 4,800 customers the optimistic end of a 301-click result (6.27%) is 6.27% + 1.645 × √(0.0627 × 0.9373 ÷ 4,800) = 6.85%, just under break-even, so 301 is the largest kill count; the 6.0% line from the first round would waste the extra precision.

The rule is deliberately asymmetric, and the asymmetry should be read plainly. Kill demands 90 per cent confidence that the true click rate falls short of break-even. Build demands only that the observed rate clear 7.0 per cent. The 0.15-point gap between 7.0 and the 6.85 break-even is not a margin for noise: the noise on 2,400 customers is about 1.645 × 0.52 = 0.86 points, so at exactly 168 clicks the one-sided 90 per cent lower bound is 7.0% − 0.86% = 6.14 per cent, below break-even. "Build" therefore means "not shown to fall short", not "shown to clear break-even"; the burden of proof was placed on the decision to stop spending. Even after the extension, 336 clicks of 4,800 (7.0%) has a lower bound of 6.39 per cent. A team that wanted the opposite burden would need a build line near 7.7 per cent on the first round, and would have to accept far more false kills.

The test ran from 15 to 28 June. Of 2,400 customers who saw the card, 131 clicked "Start auto-refill": 131 ÷ 2,400 = 5.46 per cent, which is thirteen clicks inside the kill zone. The optimistic end of the estimate is 5.46% + 1.645 × √(0.0546 × 0.9454 ÷ 2,400) = 5.46% + 0.76% = 6.22 per cent, still well short of break-even. Translating through the same chain: 5.458% × 0.40 = 2.183 per cent take-up, or about 6,987 subscribers (2.183% × 3,20,000), worth 6,987 × ₹684 ≈ ₹47.8 lakh in twelve months against ₹60 lakh of cost.

The second pass: change one input

Now change only the click-to-subscription ratio from 0.40 to 0.60, a deliberately optimistic what-if that lies above both earlier ratios (0.31 and 0.49). Break-even drops to 2.74 ÷ 0.60 = 4.57 per cent, and the observed click rate (131 ÷ 2,400 = 5.458 per cent) clears it, though not by much: its optimistic-end counterpart, the lower bound, is 5.458% − 0.763% = 4.70 per cent, only 0.13 points above 4.57. Take-up is 5.458% × 0.60 = 3.275 per cent, about 10,480 subscribers of 3,20,000, worth roughly ₹71.7 lakh against the same ₹60 lakh. The recommendation flips from kill to build, but to a thin build: under the page's own logic, a result that clears break-even by 0.13 points would earn an extension, not celebration.

The spread of the earlier ratios needs saying plainly. The 0.40 is the average of 0.31 and 0.49, and the rule ignored the spread. At 0.31 the break-even click rate is 2.74 ÷ 0.31 = 8.84 per cent, and 131 clicks is a firm kill. At 0.49 the break-even is 2.74 ÷ 0.49 = 5.59 per cent, and 131 clicks (upper bound 6.22%) would not meet the kill rule at all. So the verdict holds at the pessimistic end of the printed range and fails at the optimistic end. The statistical care taken over 6.80 against 6.85 is real but small next to this: the uncertainty about the ratio is far larger than the sampling noise the 90 per cent standard guards against. A better rule would have either pooled more earlier tests or fixed a deliberately conservative ratio, and said so.

This is the lesson of the whole example. The kill criterion did not remove judgement; it relocated it to a moment when judgement is cheap and unbiased, before the 131 was known. Had the ratio been debated after the result, the argument for 0.60 would have appeared at once and with great sincerity.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

A kill criterion is a threshold on an economic quantity, not on a metric

"Kill below 10 per cent click-through" sounds rigorous and means nothing unless the 10 came from a payback calculation. The criterion in the example traces back to ₹60 lakh, ₹684, a base of 3,20,000 and a click-to-subscription ratio of 0.40, and the last of these is the weakest input. A reader who cannot trace a threshold back to money is looking at a guess with a decimal point.

Kill, pivot and persevere are different outputs

Stopping the ₹60 lakh build is not stopping the problem. A kill criterion ends one solution to a customer need; the need may remain. Teams that treat the word "kill" as a verdict on the customer insight tend to avoid writing criteria at all, because the stakes feel personal. Write the rule about the investment, not the idea.

The grey zone must be given an action

Two zones are easy; the middle is where rules collapse. The "extend" row in the table above carries an action, and a finite one: one extension, then a closing rule at 4,800 customers with no further extension, so that "inconclusive" cannot become "carry on indefinitely".

Sample size belongs inside the rule

A threshold without a sample is not a decision rule. At 2,400 customers the optimistic end of the 6.0 per cent kill line is distinguishable from break-even only by a hair (6.80 against 6.85), which is why the result is more fragile than its precision suggests. A sample of 600 would have made the optimistic end of a 6.0 per cent reading 6.0% + 1.645 × √(0.0564 ÷ 600) = 7.6 per cent, above break-even, and the kill zone would have had to move down to about 5.3 per cent. Precision is bought with sample, and that cost belongs in the plan.

It is easy to confuse with a success metric

Success metrics describe what the team hopes for; kill criteria describe what would change its mind. They are often not the same number. In the example the success target the sales team voiced was 12 per cent. The kill line was 6.0 per cent. Teams that write only the first have no way to lose gracefully.

What a kill criterion cannot tell you

It cannot validate the measurement itself. A fake door measures stated intent among people who happened to open the app; it says nothing about customers who do not open it, or about whether the pharmacy can actually fulfil on the first of the month. A passed test removes one risk, not all of them.

Questions to ask before relying on one

Who signed it, and before what date? Where did each number come from, and how many observations stand behind it? Is the denominator everyone who was eligible and exposed? What will we do with the result in each zone, and who has authority to overrule? The ratio of 0.40 in the example came from two tests. A thoughtful newcomer notices that immediately.

6. How it differs by product type and company stage

In a consumer product, tests are fast and cheap and samples large, so criteria can be tight and numerical, as in the example. In a B2B product the samples are small: eleven pilot accounts do not support a confidence interval, so criteria tend to be behavioural and binary ("at least four of the eleven sign a paid letter of intent by 31 August; verbal enthusiasm does not count"). In a marketplace the difficulty is two-sided: a rule on buyer demand alone ignores whether supply will turn up, so the criterion needs a paired threshold, and each side is tested while the other is held artificially constant by the team.

Stage changes the stakes and the temptation. An early-stage company has few ideas and little runway, so each kill is expensive and the pressure to rationalise is intense, which is exactly why the rule must be written. A large company has many ideas and the opposite problem: projects survive because their sponsors are senior and cancellation is politically costly. There the discipline shifts from the single test to the portfolio, a theme taken up in the topic that follows this one.

7. Common mistakes

Moving the line after the result

Symptom: a test that "narrowly missed" is followed by a revised threshold in the next steering deck. Misunderstanding: that a criterion is a forecast to be refined, rather than a commitment. Cheapest diagnostic: compare the date on the signed criterion with the date of the first data pull; if the former is later, there was no criterion.

A threshold unconnected to money

Symptom: a round number (10 per cent, 1,000 sign-ups) with no derivation. Misunderstanding: that the point of the criterion is to be specific, not to be correct. Diagnostic: ask the author to recompute the threshold from the build cost; if they cannot, the number was chosen, not derived.

Treating clicks as customers

Symptom: a pitch that quotes click-through as if it were adoption. Misunderstanding: that every measured behaviour is equally costly for the customer. Diagnostic: find any earlier test of this kind that was later built, and ask what fraction of clicks became payers; if no such record exists, the ratio is an assumption and should be flagged as one.

An unowned grey zone

Symptom: results of "promising, need more data" appearing in three consecutive reviews. Misunderstanding: that ambiguity is a result. Diagnostic: look for an action in each zone of the rule; a missing action in the middle zone predicts the drift.

8. What good looks like

In the good version of the Zalmar story, which is also the version that happened, the one-page rule was dated 9 June, carried both names, and fit on a single side of paper: the assumption, the arithmetic in the order shown above, the three zones, the sample, and the sentence "If the result is 144 or fewer clicks, the build is cancelled and the ₹60 lakh returns to the pool." Nobody had to argue on 6 July, when the 131 came in. The meeting was twenty minutes long. The only discussion was about what the team would test next, which is the right discussion to have after a clean kill. A good criterion also records its own weakest input (here, the 0.40 ratio) so the reader knows where it is most fragile.

9. Closing

On Monday 6 July Vaidyanathan and Vemparala met and applied the rule as written. The result of 131 sat in the kill zone, and the ₹60 lakh build was cancelled. Vaidyanathan raised the 0.60 argument herself, in the meeting, and the two of them agreed it deserved a separate test, with a new pre-registered threshold, of whether a lighter version could reach customers more cheaply, not a reason to reopen the old one. Her reasoning was simple. The point of the signature was that it would bind the optimistic version of herself, and it would be of no use if it bound only when convenient.

What to learn next: portfolio kill criteria and stage gates, which ask how rules like this one combine when a company holds twenty live bets and a fixed budget; and, before that, a second look at designing discovery experiments, since a rule is only as good as the test beneath it.

Two questions to sit with. First, think of a project you have seen continue longer than the evidence justified: at what point could someone have written down the stopping result, and what would it have cost them socially to do so? Second, in the example the ratio of 0.40 rests on two earlier tests. How much of your own organisation's decision-making rests on a number of similar thinness, and who would notice?

Indrayani Credit Line: The Bar and the Base

An ambiguous case for discussion. Indrayani Retail Technologies, Pune, October 2026.

1. The night before

At twenty to eleven on the night of Sunday 18 October 2026, Rutika Bhave was at the dining table of her flat in Kalyani Nagar, Pune, with two versions of one slide open side by side. In Berlin it was ten past seven in the evening; in New Jersey, ten past one in the afternoon. Both carried the heading “Credit Line: criteria and result”. One showed three green ticks, the other one tick and two crosses. Neither contained a wrong figure.

At eleven the next morning she would take twelve minutes at the board meeting in Kharadi and recommend what to do about the Credit Line, a working-capital product piloted for twelve weeks with 742 borrowing kirana retailers. On Friday 26 June, three days before the pilot opened, she had signed a one-page memo with the chief executive and the chief financial officer naming three bars and one rule: all three met, the product goes to launch; any one missed, it is closed and the squad dissolved within two weeks. She had written that memo herself, and had been proud of it.

What she had not written was what the words meant. Three weeks of argument had established that the second criterion could be computed three ways, the third reported on four of the six cities, and that the partner supplying both numbers had changed its credit policy mid-pilot without formally telling her.

2. Company history, and the signature of January 2024

Indrayani Retail Technologies Private Limited was founded in Pune in 2015 by Raghav Bhagwat and a classmate from the Government College of Engineering. Its core product is route-to-market software: order capture for distributor salesmen, claims and scheme settlement for consumer-goods principals, and a retailer app for reordering stock. By September 2026 it carried 1,240 distributors and roughly 68,000 outlets, booked annual recurring revenue of ₹52 crore and employed 310 people. It had raised ₹140 crore in March 2024 from a Singapore growth fund, and held ₹46 crore of cash at 30 September against a net burn of ₹2.30 crore a month: twenty months of runway.

The decision that constrains October 2026 was taken on Thursday 11 January 2024, when Indrayani signed an exclusive origination agreement with Ikshana Capital, a Mumbai non-banking finance company. Indrayani would originate and service; Ikshana would underwrite and hold the loans on its own books, as India's digital lending framework requires. For a three-per-cent origination and servicing fee, Indrayani accepted exclusivity until 31 March 2027, a minimum cumulative disbursement of ₹75 crore by that date with a shortfall fee of 1.5 per cent of any gap, and a five-per-cent default loss guarantee held as a lien-marked deposit. The Reserve Bank of India's guidance caps such cover at five per cent of the loan portfolio; the contract's schedule computes it on principal disbursed since inception.

3. The industry

General trade still moves most packaged groceries in India, and the kirana at the end of that chain is under pressure: quick-commerce platforms such as Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart deliver in ten minutes in the same neighbourhoods; Reliance Retail's cash-and-carry, JioMart and Flipkart's wholesale arm compete for the restocking rupee; Udaan and Jumbotail sell software and stock together. Principals such as Amul, Britannia, Dabur and Parle pay for distribution visibility, and it is they, not retailers, who have paid Indrayani's bills.

Several forces made credit look obvious: UPI, on NPCI's rails, had made collections legible, with PhonePe, Paytm and Razorpay already in the retailer's day; GST e-invoicing had turned purchase records into an underwriting signal; Khatabook and OkCredit had taught retailers a digital ledger; ONDC had made demand from outside the distributor's van plausible. Against that, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 obliged Indrayani to build a consent artefact for sharing a retailer's history with a lender — work the core product now reuses for principals' analytics and would lose if the line closed.

Indrayani's exposure is not only Indian. Ishraq Markets LLC, a Dubai grocery distribution group, is its largest single contract at ₹4.80 crore of recurring revenue, a little over nine per cent of the total; it renews on 31 January 2027 against a roadmap of Arabic localisation and catalogue work nobody has started.

4. The situation in detail

In February 2026 the customer-success team interviewed 180 retailers in six cities. Asked what limited their monthly purchase, 119 of the 180 (66.1 per cent) named cash to restock; each was asked for up to three constraints and 421 were named in all. That finding started the Credit Line. What the team learned later is narrower: of 96 borrowers called back in late September, 41 said the money had gone not into stock but into giving their own customers longer credit.

The memo was signed on Friday 26 June and the pilot opened on Monday 29 June in six cities: Pune, Nashik, Nagpur, Indore, Surat and Coimbatore. Of 9,400 outlets that had placed at least eight orders in each of March, April and May, 4,000 were invited at random and the remaining 5,400 became the comparison group. Loans were twenty-one-day revolving draws against order history at a disclosed annual rate of 26 per cent. Exhibit 2 gives the funnel; Exhibit 6 the dates.

On 14 July, eighteen days after signature, Ikshana circulated the annexe whose template defines the delinquency denominator as principal disbursed since inception. Nobody objected; Rutika cannot remember reading it.

On Monday 17 August, Ikshana raised its bureau score cut-off from 680 to 710. Rupali Baindur, its chief risk officer, mentioned it in a monthly call; nobody at Indrayani logged it as a change to the experiment. Approval rates fell from 72.1 per cent in the first window to 61.2 per cent in the last, so the only cohort old enough to show thirty-day delinquency is also the one underwritten most loosely.

The pilot closed on Sunday 20 September with 1,650 loans and ₹13.20 crore disbursed. Ikshana's report of Friday 25 September put thirty-day-plus delinquency at 1.3 per cent, and the squad took that to the steering group the same afternoon. Three days later Rushikesh Bhobe, in Toronto, pointed out that a twenty-one-day loan cannot be thirty days late until fifty-one days after disbursement, so only loans disbursed by 31 July could be observed. Exhibit 3 is his table. The budget had been approved at ₹150 lakh for eight people over eight weeks; it ran to fourteen over twelve.

5. The people

Rutika Bhave, senior vice-president, product, Pune. Wrote the memo; owns Monday's recommendation. Her incentive is the second product line promised to the board for two years. She has not said she now doubts that take-up means what the memo assumed.

Raghav Bhagwat, co-founder and chief executive, Pune. Treats the memo as a promise the company made to itself, and says discipline matters more than the product. He must also explain a closed line to the fund that led the Series C, and does not say which he would give up.

Richa Bodas, chief financial officer, Pune. Signed the memo; believes a fourth criterion on unit economics was agreed on 24 June. She provisioned the guarantee at 2.5 per cent, half the cap, without telling the board it was set in July on cohort A's early behaviour.

Ranveer Bhalerao, director of engineering, Bengaluru. Nine of his engineers are on the line; six are the only ones who know the catalogue service Dubai needs. He wants a clean decision either way, and does not say a kill solves his staffing by Tuesday.

Rushikesh Bhobe, staff data scientist, Toronto. Built the seasoning analysis; will not sign a deck reporting 1.3 per cent without its base. He has an offer he has not mentioned, and has not volunteered that his 4.8 per cent rests on 21 loans.

Ravish Bhanage, head of international sales, New Jersey. Carries the Ishraq renewal; has told two Gulf prospects that catalogue work ships in the first quarter. He backs closing the line, and does not mention that his variable pay is written on renewals.

7. Voices

“1.3 per cent is not wrong, it is just not an answer. Fifty-one days is the earliest a twenty-one-day loan can be thirty days late, and on the only cohort that old we are at 4.8 per cent — about 21 loans out of 440, so four either way moves it nearly a point.” — Rushikesh Bhobe, team channel, 28 September

“Read cohort A again: it was written at a 680 cut-off we no longer use. Judging next year's book on July's loosest loans is not conservatism, it is a different error. We are ready to fund the ₹75 crore.” — Rupali Baindur, Ikshana Capital, to Rutika Bhave, 2 October

“Madam, in Nagpur the cohort A retailers are not hiding. They say the money went into giving their own customers more days. Of what is still open from that lot, all is late. My agents were paid on applications, so do not read applications as demand.” — Rajendra Bhuskute, voice note, 6 October

“We wrote the memo so this conversation would be short. If we now argue about which denominator 'book' meant, we have learned only that we argue well. And the economics bar was obviously implied.” — Raghav Bhagwat, product review, 9 October

“Ishraq signs or does not on 31 January, and the Arabic and catalogue work needs Ranveer's six people for ten weeks. I have no view on delinquency; I have a view on who is free.” — Ravish Bhanage, email, 14 October, 09:40 Eastern

“1,118 of the 1,460 applications were finished with an agent beside the retailer. Whatever 18.6 per cent measures, it is not the product. Six weeks on the flow before anyone launches.” — Ruhi Bardeskar, design review, 15 October

8. The options as Rutika sees them

She has written three on the back page of her notebook. The first is to launch across eighteen cities, since all three criteria were met as reported and the ₹75 crore commitment makes scale cheaper than retreat. It keeps the squad together, costs roughly ₹2.6 crore a quarter gross at the six-city run rate, and treats cohort A's 4.8 per cent as noise.

The second is to close the line, pay 1.5 per cent on the ₹61.80 crore shortfall — ₹92.70 lakh — release six engineers to Dubai, and tell the board the rule held. It strands the consent artefact the core product relies on, and ends the company's only non-principal revenue line.

The third is to extend by eight weeks so cohorts B and C season. That costs about ₹1.7 crore gross at the same run rate, burns eight of the twenty-three weeks left before 31 March 2027, and asks the board to accept that the memo's rule can be deferred by a vote, which Raghav calls the end of the practice. It also measures a book underwritten at 710 against a bar set for one underwritten at 680.

Nobody has written a fourth, in which Ikshana originates directly and Indrayani takes a referral fee, or a fifth, in which the criterion that failed was never the credit one but the one Ruhi keeps raising. Each of the three assumes the pilot measured the product.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at eleven on Monday 19 October, with forty minutes for the item. The contract binds: exclusivity to 31 March 2027, ₹75 crore of disbursement due by then against ₹13.20 crore done, a shortfall fee of 1.5 per cent of the gap, and a ₹66.00 lakh deposit whose base the two sides have never reconciled. The loans sit on Ikshana's books, so Indrayani cannot stop collections.

Ruhi Bardeskar's Berlin contract runs to 30 June 2027 and cannot be ended early without payment; Rushikesh Bhobe's Toronto contract runs to July 2027. Six of Ranveer's nine engineers are the only people who know the catalogue service the ₹4.80 crore Ishraq renewal depends on. Cash is ₹46 crore against a burn of ₹2.30 crore a month. And the memo dissolves the squad within two weeks of any criterion being missed.

At a quarter past midnight Rutika closed both versions of the slide and opened a blank one. She typed one line — “What we agreed to decide in advance” — and sat looking at it, unable to work out whether what followed was about the credit book, or the memo, or the six engineers who would be reassigned either way.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What, precisely, did the memo of 26 June commit Indrayani to? Which of its criteria could have been computed, on 26 June, from data the pilot would produce?
  2. Using Exhibits 2 and 3 only, which denominator should criterion 2 have named, and who had the standing to choose it?
  3. Exhibit 1's third result rests on four of the six cities. What must you believe about Indore and Surat to accept it, and what does Exhibit 4 say?
  4. Ikshana raised its cut-off on 17 August. What does that do to the comparison between cohort A and the rest, and to the value of an extension?
  5. Exhibit 5 was never a criterion. Should it have been? Work through the board meeting if Richa's recollection of 24 June is right, and then if Raghav's is.
  6. What should Rutika Bhave do on Monday morning, and what exactly should she say to the board about the memo she signed on 26 June?

Hastakshar Collect: The Rule Written Before the Test

A decision case on kill criteria and decision rules

1. Opening

On Friday 23 October 2026, just before six, Pradnya Ashtekar closed the door of a small meeting room in Hastakshar's office in Baner, Pune, and dialled in four colleagues. It was 8:30 in the morning in Toronto and New Jersey, 2:30 in the afternoon in Berlin and 8:30 at night in Singapore. As Vice President of Product she had run a six-week experiment on a feature called Hastakshar Collect, which ended on Sunday 18 October. On Monday 26 October at half past ten she would recommend one of three courses to the steering committee.

She had the numbers. What she lacked was agreement on what they meant, and the one document signed before the test began was now remembered differently by two of its signatories.

2. Company background

Hastakshar Technologies was founded in 2016 in Pune by Prakash Agarkar and two classmates from the College of Engineering, Pune. It sells electronic signature and document workflow software to small and mid-sized Indian businesses: distributors, staffing firms, clinics and builders' offices that need purchase orders and offer letters signed without a courier. It has 5,400 paying accounts, annual recurring revenue of ₹38 crore and 74 employees.

Leegality and Digio compete directly in signatures, and Zoho Sign comes bundled with Zoho's suite. Getting paid is more crowded still: Razorpay Payment Links, Khatabook and Tally all touch the invoice. Yet when Hastakshar's customer-success team interviewed customers in early 2026, a pattern kept surfacing. Signing was not their problem. Collecting was.

3. The situation

Hastakshar Collect attaches to an invoice and sends WhatsApp reminders before and after the due date, each carrying a UPI payment link. The planned price was ₹1,299 per account per month. A team of six built it: four engineers in Pune and Bengaluru, a designer in Berlin, Prasun Aphale, and a data scientist in Toronto, Pritesh Akerkar. Work began on Monday 29 June and the test opened on Monday 7 September, so by 18 October the team had spent 16 weeks. At ₹1 lakh per person-week, the finance team's loaded average, that is ₹96 lakh.

On Friday 4 September, three days before launch, Pradnya, Prakash and Pritesh signed a one-page memo naming three bars and one rule: continue only if all three are met; if any one is missed, the idea is closed. The test drew 600 accounts at random from the 3,000 that had signed at least ten invoice-linked documents the previous quarter; 400 were offered Collect and 200 held out. Exhibit 1 sets each bar beside its result.

4. The people

Prakash Agarkar, chief executive, Pune. On Thursday evening he messaged Pradnya that "we said five points, and we got five." He wants to ship. The memo, which Pradnya has in front of her, says eight, and Pritesh's analysis plan from the same day says eight as well.

Pritesh Akerkar, data scientist, Toronto. He designed the hold-out and wrote the analysis plan. He regards 5.0 points as flattering, for the reason in the footnote to Exhibit 2, and doubts the size split: thirty accounts, examined after the result.

Purnima Argade, customer-success lead, Singapore. Her team talks to the 112 activated accounts weekly, and 70 are still sending reminders. She worries about trust if Hastakshar switches off something customers rely on, and about consent, since the reminders reach customers' own debtors under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act.

Pratik Almeida, head of sales, New Jersey. A Dubai-headquartered electronics distributor, 1.5 hours behind Pune, has said it would take Collect for 60 of its Indian dealers. Pratik wants a launch date.

5. The options

Pradnya has sketched three courses, costed in Exhibit 4.

People cost is people times weeks at ₹1 lakh per person-week; Total is People cost plus Messaging. Option C is one setup week plus four test weeks, and its read-out counts invoices raised in the first two. The ₹96 lakh spent is sunk in all three.

Option A: apply the rule. Close Collect, switch it off for active accounts after notice, and return all six people to the signature roadmap after a two-week wind-down by three of them. The upside is a rule that still means something next time, for ₹6 lakh. The cost is the large-invoice signal left unexplored, hard conversations with customers, and a chief executive who must accept a verdict he disputed.

Option B: extend and relax. Run six more weeks and accept 5 points as a pass. The upside is more data and peace with Prakash. The cost is ₹39 lakh and a bar moved to fit the result, which turns the memo into a formality.

Option C: close, then retest narrowly. Declare the original idea closed, then run one four-week test on accounts with average invoices of ₹50,000 and above, with new criteria signed first. The upside is a sharper answer on the one promising signal for ₹16 lakh. The cost is five weeks of half a team and the risk of looking like Option B renamed.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Which bars in the 4 September memo did the test meet, which did it miss, and what does the memo's own rule require?
  2. Prakash remembers a five-point bar while the memo says eight. What does that gap say about why a kill criterion must be written down in advance?
  3. Exhibit 2 shows a 14.1-point uplift among large-invoice accounts. How much weight should a split chosen after the result carry, and what would make it credible?
  4. Which option would you recommend, and what would you commit in writing before running any further test?

7. A note for the learner

This topic asks one question of any experiment: what result would make us stop, and did we decide that before running it? A kill criterion is a number and a consequence written down in advance and agreed by the people who would most like to ignore it. It makes the decision cheap at the moment the evidence arrives, when hope and sunk cost push the other way.

A well-reasoned answer begins by reading the rule as written. Two bars were met and the uplift bar was missed by three points, so the idea as specified is closed. Even the 5.0 points deserves scepticism. Prakash's recollection shows how easily a threshold drifts once the result is known.

One defensible path is Option C, taken in this order. First, tell the committee that Collect as specified fails its own test and close it, switching off the 70 active accounts with notice. Second, treat the 14.1-point finding as a new hypothesis, not a rescue: it came from one cut of thirty accounts, examined after the fact. Third, authorise a single four-week retest costing ₹16 lakh on fresh accounts with average invoices of ₹50,000 and above, comparing everyone offered against everyone held out so self-selection cannot flatter the result. Fourth, sign the bars before launch, for example activation of at least 30 per cent, uplift of at least 10 points and week-six retention of at least 60 per cent, with any miss ending the idea for good.

A rough size of the prize: at the pilot's rates, 3,000 accounts with 28 per cent activation and 62.5 per cent retention would leave 525 accounts still sending reminders, worth about ₹82 lakh a year if all paid the planned ₹1,299 a month. That sizes the original design, not Option C's narrower one. Option B spends ₹39 lakh on a product of that size; Option C spends ₹16 lakh and ends on Monday 7 December either way. Diwali falls on 8 November, but both arms of the retest see the same festival, so the hold-out protects it. Option A is also defensible. Option B is not, because it moves the bar after the number is known.
